metadata.title: Integration Hell
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 10 — why Continuous Integration exists: months of divergence made merge day a catastrophe, frequent merges plus an automated gauntlet made it routine, and a green pipeline is only ever as strong as the assertions inside it.

metadata.series_note: Week 7 (claude-stem-ci-for-ai, 'The Regression Problem') already covered CI *for AI specifically* — non-determinism, regression suites, the blocked merge. This reel is deliberately the OTHER half: why CI exists at all, what merge cadence has to do with it, and where a green pipeline stops being evidence. The AI beat is kept short and framed as a callback.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. In the early days of software engineering, developers wrote code on their own laptops for months, and then tried to merge all of it together on deployment day. The result was known, affectionately, as Integration Hell — where conflicting code took down production. Modern engineering avoids it with a philosophy called Continuous Integration.
beats.new_visual_element: Cold open — the cost of waiting to merge

props.command: Six teams branched off main three months ago. We merge on Friday. What actually happens on Friday?
output: Every conflict is three months stale.
Nobody remembers why either side is right.

beats.honesty_note: The scenario is illustrative of the pre-CI working style the script describes; no specific project is being reported.

beats.narration_text: Merging is not the hard part. Waiting to merge is the hard part — and everything Continuous Integration does follows from refusing to wait. The frequency is the technique.

props.text:
Merging hurts.
So do it far more often.

beats.authoring_note: Both readings are true sentences: 'Merging hurts.' and, corrected, 'Waiting hurts.' — the correction IS the thesis.

beats.narration_text: Continuous Integration is the practice of merging changes into one shared repository very frequently — often several times a day. The cost of a merge grows with how long you waited, so you stop waiting. But you do not simply dump the code in. Every push is intercepted by an automated server before it is allowed to land. That server is a bouncer, and it does not care whose code it is.
beats.new_visual_element: Three months of divergence against one afternoon

props.stampSub: the merge is small because the wait was short

beats.honesty_note: 4,812 files / 31 conflicts / 14 files are illustrative magnitudes chosen to show the shape of the difference, not measurements of any repository.

beats.narration_text: The server forces every push through an automated gauntlet. It checks the formatting. It runs the unit tests, to establish that what already worked still works. It scans the dependencies for known vulnerabilities. And it builds the deployment container from scratch, on a machine that has never seen your laptop. If any step fails, the pipeline halts and the code does not land.

beats.act: SCENE 4 — WHY AI NEEDS IT MORE
beats.narration_text: For A.I. systems this stops being good practice and starts being necessary. I made a whole video about why — the short version is that an A.I. system has moving parts that are not code. Change a prompt, swap an embedding model, re-index a vector store, and nothing in the diff looks dangerous. The regression suite is the only thing standing between that edit and production.
beats.new_visual_element: The merge that gets blocked by a prompt edit

show.event: PR panel reveals; the diff is three lines of prompt text
checks begin counting up
the count stops short — the regression suite disagrees
the button stays MERGE BLOCKED and never arms

props.sparkLine: Nothing in this diff looks dangerous.
props.code:
- Answer only from the retrieved ledger rows.
- If the rows do not support the claim, say so.
+ Answer from the retrieved ledger rows.
+ Be helpful and concise.

# three lines. no code changed.
# 11 regression cases now fail.

beats.honesty_note: neverArms is set because this beat narrates a BLOCKED merge; without it the button flips to ALL CHECKS PASSED on elapsed time and contradicts the narration. The diff and the case counts are illustrative. Deliberately short — Week 7's reel is the long version of this argument.
beats.authoring_note: The dropped line is the one that forbids answering beyond the retrieved rows — that is why a cosmetic prompt tidy-up breaks eleven cases.

beats.narration_text: So where does this break? A green pipeline is not evidence that the code works. It is evidence that nothing you wrote a test for is broken — which is a much smaller claim. The gauntlet runs your assertions, and it cannot run the ones you never wrote. Worse, a test that calls a function and only checks that it did not crash will pass against a function that does nothing at all. Count assertions, not checkmarks.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED. The supplied script treats a passing pipeline as proof of correctness ('force it to prove it works'). It proves the assertions held. This beat also sets up the companion Provenance Gatekeeper reel, where a test passed against a function that only printed a success message.

beats.narration_text: So stop hoping your code works. Make it prove it — on a machine that is not yours, before it reaches anyone else. And write the assertion that would fail if the function did nothing.

props.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml
props.code:
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gauntlet:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: pytest -q
      - run: pip-audit
      - run: docker build .

# TASK: build the gauntlet.
# Then make one test fail on purpose.

beats.authoring_note: 'Make one test fail on purpose' is the reel's addition — an untested pipeline is a pipeline nobody has seen say no.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own suite. Ask a model which of your tests would still pass if the function it tests were replaced with one that returns immediately and does nothing. Every test it names is a test that is not holding anything up.
beats.new_visual_element: Handoff — the viewer's prompt, read aloud

show.event: composer reframes; greeting reads 'Your turn.'

props.command: Here is my test file. Which of these tests would STILL PASS if the function under test were replaced by one that returns immediately and does nothing? List them, and say what assertion each one is missing.

beats.narration_text: Merge early, merge often — and count assertions, not checkmarks. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
